thesis: The cellular aging supplement market runs on a confidence trick: blur the line between one compound with gold-standard human data and others with preliminary open-label scraps, then sell all three at the same premium price point.
stakes: If you're shopping for longevity supplements, the evidence gap between the best and worst options in the same 'stack' is enormous — and the marketers are banking on you not knowing which is which.
counterpoint: Weak evidence is not the same as no evidence — GlyNAC's open-label results are genuinely intriguing, and dismissing early-stage research because it lacks blinding would kill promising interventions before they can be properly tested.
implication: Before you spend money on any supplement marketed for aging, look up the trial design yourself: if the pivotal study is open-label with no placebo control from the same lab that invented the supplement, your confidence should drop accordingly.
close: Dr. Burridge hid the supplement names for a reason — because once you see the labels, the stack stops looking like a stack and starts looking like one real thing riding shotgun with two gamblers. The next time someone sells you a longevity protocol bundled in a neat little package, remember that image: three bottles, one with a real trial behind it, two with hope and a Baylor phone number. Read the fine print before you swallow anything.
